I find the Monkees a really interesting part of rock history. They were one of the first major collusions of "the industry" and musicians. Riding the wave of the Beatles, a still young television industry tried to use the head-spinning phenomenon of the Beatles as a product for themselves. So many people trying to grab a piece of the pie. Tork and Nesmith, who were actually musicians, paired with two actors (Jones and Dolenz) hired to make a show about a band. The problems came about when the actual music interests were forced to meld with the commercial interests of entertainment. Shoved into the wrong roles for an actual band. Tork was the better guitarist/keyboardist, Nesmith, a bassist, was into more of a country vein, Dolenz the better singer, and Jones was the best, but not that good, drummer of the four. But their positions were dictated by how they were developed as characters for a tv show.

Mainly due to Nesmith and Tork, they did in fact develop into a real working band of sorts, eventually exerting more control over the music produced. More and more of their songs were written by them, and they became much more proficient in their musical abilities. The list of people that became involved with them was stunning, from the Beatles themselves, Jack Nicholson, Frank Zappa, Stephen Stills, Harry Nilsson, Lowell George, Buddy Miles, and Neil Young. It really was a struggle for them, being a very public "battle" between commercialism and musical integrity. The battle was always a part of recorded music, with the noted Tom Petty situations being a recent more public example. The Monkees do deserve more credit than they were given for being early 'warriors' in those battles.

And just a small note: Newspapers and magazines reported that the Monkees outsold the Beatles and the Rolling Stones combined in 1967, but Nesmith claims in his autobiography Infinite Tuesday that it was a lie that he told a reporter. I sometimes wonder which is more prolific, the myths and 'enhancements' made by marketing and artists (to that end) or the actual stories behind our beloved music.
